screens.title: Implementing Core Game Systems
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you'll learn how a small set of core systems—player controls, enemy behavior, and UI—work together to create playable scenes in Unity. We'll focus on writing clear C# components, choosing appropriate movement primitives like Rigidbody or CharacterController, using simple state machines for enemies, and wiring UI through events so systems remain decoupled. I will guide you through concrete code examples that implement movement, jumping, a patrol-chase enemy, and an event-driven health display. You will see why separating input handling from movement logic matters, how a three-state enemy reduces complexity, and how UnityEvent lets UI respond without tight coupling. As you follow along, think about maintainability: smaller components that communicate through events or interfaces are easier to test, replace, and reuse across scenes. By the end of this lesson you'll be ready to implement these systems in your capstone scene and confidently extend them, for example adding a new enemy state or swapping a health display for an animated bar. What will you refactor first once your systems are decoupled?

Implementing Core Game Systems

Translate your GDD into player movement, enemy state machines, and responsive UI. Examples use Unity C# and UnityEvent patterns to keep systems loosely coupled.

In this lesson
Implement movement, jumping, and input separation so your player feels responsive.
Coming up
Build a patrol-chase enemy using a simple state machine and transitions.
Hands-on
Wire a PlayerHealth UnityEvent to a UIManager to update the health display without direct calls.
Why this matters

Clear separation and event-driven updates prevent hard-to-maintain code and reduce bugs when roles change or systems are reused in other scenes.

Quick concept map
Player → InputManager → Movement; Enemy → StateMachine → Transitions; PlayerHealth → UnityEvent → UIManager.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These four objectives map to concrete skills you'll demonstrate. First, designing and implementing robust player control systems ensures the character responds predictably across inputs and physics settings. You will separate input detection from movement logic so swapping input systems is simple. Second, you will develop basic enemy AI behaviors using state machines: patrol, chase, and attack. That structure keeps behavior predictable and easy to extend. Third, you'll integrate UI elements that display health and score, and you'll wire them to game systems using UnityEvent so updates are immediate and decoupled. Finally, you'll apply principles of decoupled system design—using events or interfaces—to let systems communicate without direct references. Each objective includes a verification milestone, such as a working PlayerHealth event that updates a TextMeshPro display when damage occurs. Practically, you'll run a simple scene where the player can take damage and an enemy will chase when nearby, proving systems work together. Keep these objectives in mind as check-points while you implement and test your capstone elements.

screens.title: Designing Player Controls
screens.narratorSegment: Designing player controls begins with a simple principle: separate the detection of input from the code that moves the character. Doing so allows you to swap input sources—keyboard, gamepad, or mobile touch—without changing movement physics or animation logic. Practically, you can create an InputManager that reads input axes or action callbacks, then forwards a clean set of values to a PlayerMovement component. PlayerMovement interprets those values and applies translation, forces, or CharacterController commands. In Unity, movement commonly uses either a Rigidbody for physics-driven motion or a CharacterController for kinematic movement; each requires different handling of collisions and jumping. Implementing a clear interface between input and movement helps when you later add features like sprinting, slope handling, or networked input: you update InputManager or PlayerMovement independently. A common misconception is to place input and movement in a single script, which makes tuning and reusing harder. For example, if you later want to test AI-driven movement, you'd need to extract movement code anyway. A quick verification: replace player input with automated values and confirm movement behaves the same. That check proves your separation worked and makes future changes safer.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Designing Player Controls
Pattern

InputManager → PlayerMovement

A small InputManager reads axes or actions and sends normalized values, while PlayerMovement focuses on physics and animation.

Why separate?
  • Makes swapping input systems painless.
  • Simplifies automated tests and AI-driven movement.
  • Keeps responsibilities small and clear.
Common mistake

Putting input checks and rigidbody updates in the same Update loop causes tight coupling and makes reuse difficult.

Process Flow
1
Capture Input
Read axes or action callbacks in InputManager.
2
Normalize Data
Convert raw inputs to movement vectors or commands.
3
Apply Movement
PlayerMovement applies translation, forces, or controller moves.
Key Takeaway

Separation makes testing and extension easier—swap inputs or inject AI movement without changing physics code.

screens.title: PlayerMovement Walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a simple Rigidbody-based PlayerMovement script to highlight concrete responsibilities. The example uses a Rigidbody for physics, handles horizontal movement with Input. GetAxis, and adds an impulse for jumping. First, the Start method caches the Rigidbody component; this avoids repeated GetComponent calls and improves performance. In Update you collect horizontal and vertical input and compute a movement vector. The script uses transform. Translate for position change and rb. AddForce for jumping, which mixes kinematic translation with physics impulses—an approach that works for many prototypes but requires care: moving the transform directly can bypass collision responses, so ensure your collision model matches the intended behavior. The OnCollisionEnter sets isGrounded when landing on objects tagged "Ground"; remember to tag your ground meshes. A common misconception is that transform. Translate is always safe with a Rigidbody—while it moves the object, it may not properly interact with physics in all cases. A better pattern for physics-driven chars is to use rb. MovePosition or apply velocities consistently. Use this script as a starting point, then refactor movement to be fully physics-driven or fully kinematic depending on your gameplay needs. Which approach fits your design better—responsive arcade movement or simulated physics?

keyIdea.title: Script Responsibility
keyIdea.text: Cache components, separate input capture, and choose consistent movement method (kinematic vs physics) to avoid conflicts.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › PlayerMovement Walkthrough
Code Example
// PlayerMovement.cs
using UnityEngine;

public class PlayerMovement : MonoBehaviour
{
  public float moveSpeed = 5f;
  public float jumpForce = 10f;
  private Rigidbody rb;
  private bool isGrounded;

  void Start()
  {
    rb = GetComponent<Rigidbody>();
  }

  void Update()
  {
    float horizontalInput = Input.GetAxis("Horizontal");
    float verticalInput = Input.GetAxis("Vertical");

    Vector3 movement = new Vector3(horizontalInput, 0f, verticalInput) * moveSpeed * Time.deltaTime;
    transform.Translate(movement);

    if (Input.GetButtonDown("Jump") && isGrounded)
    {
      rb.AddForce(Vector3.up * jumpForce, ForceMode.Impulse);
      isGrounded = false;
    }
  }

  void OnCollisionEnter(Collision collision)
  {
    if (collision.gameObject.CompareTag("Ground"))
    {
      isGrounded = true;
    }
  }
}
Explanation
  • Start caches Rigidbody to avoid repeated component lookups.
  • Update reads input and applies transform.Translate for immediate movement.
  • Jump uses AddForce to push the body upward; grounding uses collision tags.
Pro tip

Prefer rb.MovePosition or velocity updates for consistent physics interaction. If using transform-based moves, avoid physics-based collisions for the same object.

Key Takeaway

Choose one movement model and keep inputs separate for easier refactor and reliable collision behavior.

screens.title: Rigidbody vs CharacterController
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between Rigidbody and CharacterController depends on your gameplay goals. Use Rigidbody when you want objects to respond to forces, gravity, and collisions in a simulated way—platformers with momentum or interactions with other physics objects benefit from Rigidbody-driven motion. CharacterController is preferable when you need precise, kinematic control and predictable collision without full physics simulation, such as third-person adventure games where you script exact steps, slopes, and root-motion animation. Rigidbody moves are generally driven by forces, velocities, or MovePosition, and require consistent physics updates; mixing transform. Translate calls with Rigidbody forces can cause unexpected behavior. CharacterController. Move is a kinematic A P I that expects you to manage gravity and collisions through its built-in methods, which can simplify code but reduce realistic physics responses. A common misconception is that Rigidbody always provides better movement realism; in practice it introduces complexity when you need deterministic or tightly tuned movement. Test both: prototype with CharacterController for tight control, switch to Rigidbody when environmental physics interactions are necessary. The right choice simplifies the rest of your system design. Rigidbody vs CharacterController means rigidbody for physics interactions and momentum; charactercontroller for precise, kinematic character movement without full physics.. In practical terms, when to choose physics-driven motion versus kinematic movement.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Rigidbody vs CharacterController
Rigidbody
  • Physics-driven, responds to forces, gravity, collisions.
  • Use AddForce, velocity, or MovePosition for consistent behavior.
  • Great for momentum, realistic interactions with other physics objects.
Watch out: mixing transform.Translate with Rigidbody can bypass physics.
CharacterController
  • Kinematic movement, precise control, built-in collision handling.
  • Call CharacterController.Move and manage gravity in your code.
  • Ideal for tightly controlled player movement and animation-driven locomotion.
Tip: use CharacterController for deterministic gameplay where physics feel is not required.
Decision Checklist
Need momentum? Choose Rigidbody.
Need precise animation sync? Choose CharacterController.
Prototype both and measure feel against design goals.

screens.title: Enemy AI with State Machines
screens.narratorSegment: Enemy behavior is often best expressed as a small state machine. Define explicit states—Patrol, Chase, Attack—and the conditions that move the enemy between them. Patrol moves between waypoints at patrolSpeed; when the player enters detectionRange, transition to Chase at a higher speed. If the player gets within attackRange, transition to Attack to play animations or apply damage. Also define escape transitions: if the player moves beyond detectionRange plus a buffer, transition back to Patrol. This structure clarifies behavior, reduces conditional spaghetti code, and makes debugging straightforward—each state encapsulates one responsibility. Implement transitions with simple distance checks in Update or via trigger events for better performance. A common misconception is that state machines are heavyweight; small enums and a switch statement are sufficient for many games. Log state changes with Debug. Log during development to observe transitions and tune ranges. In capstone work, a well-structured state machine makes it easy to add behaviors like Flee, Search, or Alert later without rewriting core logic. Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Enemy AI with State Machines
State Layout
Patrol — move between waypoints
Chase — move towards player when detected
Attack — close-range behavior and damage

Transitions are typically based on distance checks, line-of-sight, or timers. Keep transition guards simple and test them with Debug.Log to verify behavior during tuning.

Example Conditions
  • if distanceToPlayer < detectionRange → Chase
  • if distanceToPlayer < attackRange → Attack
  • if distanceToPlayer > detectionRange + 2 → Patrol
Common-mistake
Packing patrol, chase, and attack logic into a single long Update method makes state changes hard to reason about and debug.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › EnemyAI Walkthrough
Code Example
// EnemyAI.cs
using UnityEngine;

public class EnemyAI : MonoBehaviour
{
  public enum EnemyState { Patrol, Chase, Attack }
  public EnemyState currentState = EnemyState.Patrol;

  public float patrolSpeed = 2f;
  public float chaseSpeed = 4f;
  public float detectionRange = 10f;
  public float attackRange = 2f;
  public Transform playerTransform; // Assign player in inspector

  void Update()
  {
    float distanceToPlayer = Vector3.Distance(transform.position, playerTransform.position);

    switch (currentState)
    {
      case EnemyState.Patrol:
        // Implement patrol logic
        if (distanceToPlayer < detectionRange)
          currentState = EnemyState.Chase;
        break;
      case EnemyState.Chase:
        transform.position = Vector3.MoveTowards(transform.position, playerTransform.position, chaseSpeed * Time.deltaTime);
        if (distanceToPlayer < attackRange)
          currentState = EnemyState.Attack;
        else if (distanceToPlayer > detectionRange + 2f)
          currentState = EnemyState.Patrol;
        break;
      case EnemyState.Attack:
        // Implement attack logic
        if (distanceToPlayer > attackRange)
          currentState = EnemyState.Chase;
        break;
    }
  }
}
Explanation
  • The enum defines discrete states for clarity and readability.
  • Distance checks drive transitions; a small buffer prevents rapid toggles.
  • Each state should encapsulate movement and animation concerns.
Debugging tip

Add Debug.Log with currentState to observe transitions. Tune detection and attack ranges in play mode for desired feel.

Pro Tip

Keep patrol waypoints and pathfinding separate from state logic so you can reuse the same states with different navigation systems.

screens.title: Decoupled System Design
screens.narratorSegment: Decoupled system design means components communicate through well-defined contracts rather than direct references. In Unity that often looks like events—UnityEvent or C# events—or interfaces that declare behavior without tying code to concrete types. For example, a PlayerHealth component can expose an OnHealthChanged UnityEvent; any UI component can subscribe and update its display without PlayerHealth knowing about UIManager. This reduces tight coupling: you can replace UIManager with a different implementation or add other listeners like audio cues and save systems with minimal change. A common mistake is to have PlayerHealth call UIManager. UpdateHealthBar directly; that creates a hard dependency and makes reuse difficult. Using interfaces is another option: a damageable interface lets damage sources call TakeDamage without knowing player internals. Decoupling also supports unit testing because you can supply mock listeners instead of real UI in test scenes. The practical sign of good decoupling is that swapping components should require only inspector wiring, not code edits. Which listeners will you add to your PlayerHealth event during testing? This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Decoupled System Design
Pattern

Use UnityEvent or C# events to broadcast changes. Let receivers subscribe rather than calling receivers directly.

Benefits
  • Fewer dependencies between scripts.
  • Easier to add listeners like sound, UI, or analytics.
  • Safer refactors and faster iteration.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › PlayerHealth and UnityEvent
PlayerHealth (starter)
using UnityEngine;
using UnityEngine.Events;

public class PlayerHealth : MonoBehaviour
{
  public int maxHealth = 100;
  private int currentHealth;

  public UnityEvent<int> OnHealthChanged = new UnityEvent<int>();

  void Start()
  {
    currentHealth = maxHealth;
    OnHealthChanged.Invoke(currentHealth);
  }

  public void TakeDamage(int amount)
  {
    currentHealth -= amount;
    currentHealth = Mathf.Max(0, currentHealth);
    OnHealthChanged.Invoke(currentHealth);

    if (currentHealth <= 0)
      Die();
  }

  private void Die()
  {
    Debug.Log("Player Died!");
  }
}
UIManager hookup

In the Inspector, add the UIManager.UpdateHealthUI method to OnHealthChanged. Alternatively subscribe in Start with AddListener, and unsubscribe in OnDestroy to avoid leaks.

Testing tip

Trigger TakeDamage via a test key or a cheater object to verify the UI updates and Die is called when health reaches zero.

Key Takeaway

Events let multiple systems react to health changes without PlayerHealth needing direct references to them.

screens.title: Common Pitfalls and Debugging Tips
screens.narratorSegment: When building these systems you'll encounter recurring pitfalls. First, tight coupling happens when scripts call each other directly; avoid placing UI updates inside gameplay scripts. Use UnityEvent or interfaces instead. Second, continuous polling of other components in Update is inefficient and brittle—subscribe to events where possible. Third, mixing transform-based translation with Rigidbody physics can cause collisions to behave oddly; choose a single motion model per object. Fourth, forgetting to unsubscribe listeners before destroying objects may lead to null reference exceptions or lingering callbacks; remove listeners in OnDestroy or use inspector-only subscriptions. Fifth, incorrect grounding checks—such as relying on tag-less objects—will break jumping; ensure ground objects carry the correct tag or use layer masks. For debugging, add Debug. Log statements for state transitions and event invocations, use the inspector to watch values, and test on multiple resolutions to validate UI. Tuning is iterative: adjust speeds, ranges, and UI anchor points until the gameplay feel matches your design goals. Which pitfall will you prioritize eliminating in your first playtest? fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you'll learn how a small set of core systems—player controls, enemy behavior, and UI—work together to create playable scenes in Unity. We'll focus on writing clear C# components, choosing appropriate movement primitives like Rigidbody or CharacterController, using simple state machines for enemies, and wiring UI through events so systems remain decoupled. I will guide you through concrete code examples that implement movement, jumping, a patrol-chase enemy, and an event-driven health display. You will see why separating input handling from movement logic matters, how a three-state enemy reduces complexity, and how UnityEvent lets UI respond without tight coupling. As you follow along, think about maintainability: smaller components that communicate through events or interfaces are easier to test, replace, and reuse across scenes. By the end of this lesson you'll be ready to implement these systems in your capstone scene and confidently extend them, for example adding a new enemy state or swapping a health display for an animated bar. What will you refactor first once your systems are decoupled?

These four objectives map to concrete skills you'll demonstrate. First, designing and implementing robust player control systems ensures the character responds predictably across inputs and physics settings. You will separate input detection from movement logic so swapping input systems is simple. Second, you will develop basic enemy AI behaviors using state machines: patrol, chase, and attack. That structure keeps behavior predictable and easy to extend. Third, you'll integrate UI elements that display health and score, and you'll wire them to game systems using UnityEvent so updates are immediate and decoupled. Finally, you'll apply principles of decoupled system design—using events or interfaces—to let systems communicate without direct references. Each objective includes a verification milestone, such as a working PlayerHealth event that updates a TextMeshPro display when damage occurs. Practically, you'll run a simple scene where the player can take damage and an enemy will chase when nearby, proving systems work together. Keep these objectives in mind as check-points while you implement and test your capstone elements.

This second objectives screen focuses on the practical checks you will run. For player control, verify the player has expected acceleration, deceleration, and reliable jumping by testing with a few Rigidbody settings or CharacterController behaviors. For enemy AI, log state changes so you can see exactly when patrol becomes chase. That visibility will help you tune detectionRange and attackRange. For UI, hook the PlayerHealth UnityEvent in the Inspector to your UIManager method and confirm the health text updates immediately when TakeDamage is called. Finally, check decoupling by trying to replace the UIManager with a stubbed display object; if the system is properly event-driven, you only need to subscribe to the event and not change PlayerHealth. These verification steps matter because they show your systems are modular: you can swap components, tune parameters, and extend behavior with minimal rework. Run the hands-on activity and treat these checks as acceptance criteria for a deliverable scene.

Designing player controls begins with a simple principle: separate the detection of input from the code that moves the character. Doing so allows you to swap input sources—keyboard, gamepad, or mobile touch—without changing movement physics or animation logic. Practically, you can create an InputManager that reads input axes or action callbacks, then forwards a clean set of values to a PlayerMovement component. PlayerMovement interprets those values and applies translation, forces, or CharacterController commands. In Unity, movement commonly uses either a Rigidbody for physics-driven motion or a CharacterController for kinematic movement; each requires different handling of collisions and jumping. Implementing a clear interface between input and movement helps when you later add features like sprinting, slope handling, or networked input: you update InputManager or PlayerMovement independently. A common misconception is to place input and movement in a single script, which makes tuning and reusing harder. For example, if you later want to test AI-driven movement, you'd need to extract movement code anyway. A quick verification: replace player input with automated values and confirm movement behaves the same. That check proves your separation worked and makes future changes safer.

Let's walk through a simple Rigidbody-based PlayerMovement script to highlight concrete responsibilities. The example uses a Rigidbody for physics, handles horizontal movement with Input. GetAxis, and adds an impulse for jumping. First, the Start method caches the Rigidbody component; this avoids repeated GetComponent calls and improves performance. In Update you collect horizontal and vertical input and compute a movement vector. The script uses transform. Translate for position change and rb. AddForce for jumping, which mixes kinematic translation with physics impulses—an approach that works for many prototypes but requires care: moving the transform directly can bypass collision responses, so ensure your collision model matches the intended behavior. The OnCollisionEnter sets isGrounded when landing on objects tagged "Ground"; remember to tag your ground meshes. A common misconception is that transform. Translate is always safe with a Rigidbody—while it moves the object, it may not properly interact with physics in all cases. A better pattern for physics-driven chars is to use rb. MovePosition or apply velocities consistently. Use this script as a starting point, then refactor movement to be fully physics-driven or fully kinematic depending on your gameplay needs. Which approach fits your design better—responsive arcade movement or simulated physics?

Choosing between Rigidbody and CharacterController depends on your gameplay goals. Use Rigidbody when you want objects to respond to forces, gravity, and collisions in a simulated way—platformers with momentum or interactions with other physics objects benefit from Rigidbody-driven motion. CharacterController is preferable when you need precise, kinematic control and predictable collision without full physics simulation, such as third-person adventure games where you script exact steps, slopes, and root-motion animation. Rigidbody moves are generally driven by forces, velocities, or MovePosition, and require consistent physics updates; mixing transform. Translate calls with Rigidbody forces can cause unexpected behavior. CharacterController. Move is a kinematic A P I that expects you to manage gravity and collisions through its built-in methods, which can simplify code but reduce realistic physics responses. A common misconception is that Rigidbody always provides better movement realism; in practice it introduces complexity when you need deterministic or tightly tuned movement. Test both: prototype with CharacterController for tight control, switch to Rigidbody when environmental physics interactions are necessary. The right choice simplifies the rest of your system design. Rigidbody vs CharacterController means rigidbody for physics interactions and momentum; charactercontroller for precise, kinematic character movement without full physics.. In practical terms, when to choose physics-driven motion versus kinematic movement.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Enemy behavior is often best expressed as a small state machine. Define explicit states—Patrol, Chase, Attack—and the conditions that move the enemy between them. Patrol moves between waypoints at patrolSpeed; when the player enters detectionRange, transition to Chase at a higher speed. If the player gets within attackRange, transition to Attack to play animations or apply damage. Also define escape transitions: if the player moves beyond detectionRange plus a buffer, transition back to Patrol. This structure clarifies behavior, reduces conditional spaghetti code, and makes debugging straightforward—each state encapsulates one responsibility. Implement transitions with simple distance checks in Update or via trigger events for better performance. A common misconception is that state machines are heavyweight; small enums and a switch statement are sufficient for many games. Log state changes with Debug. Log during development to observe transitions and tune ranges. In capstone work, a well-structured state machine makes it easy to add behaviors like Flee, Search, or Alert later without rewriting core logic. Enemy AI with State Machines means use explicit states and clear transition conditions to keep ai predictable and extensible.. In practical terms, design states and clear transitions for predictable behavior.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Now let's read a concise EnemyAI example implementing the three-state pattern. The script exposes parameters for patrolSpeed, chaseSpeed, detectionRange, and attackRange, and it requires a reference to the player's Transform. In Update we compute the distance to player and use a switch on the currentState enum to select behavior. Patrol logic moves between waypoints; on detection it sets currentState to Chase. Chase moves toward the player and checks for attackRange to enter Attack. Attack handles damage or animations and checks for distance to return to Chase. Notice the escape guard that returns to Patrol when the player escapes beyond detectionRange plus a small buffer; this prevents rapid flicker between states when the player is at the edge of detection. A useful development technique is to add Debug. Log messages inside each case so you can see transitions in the Console. When you later add features like pathfinding or animation events, keep those concerns inside their state case to preserve clarity. Decoupled system design means components communicate through well-defined contracts rather than direct references. In Unity that often looks like events—UnityEvent or C# events—or interfaces that declare behavior without tying code to concrete types. For example, a PlayerHealth component can expose an OnHealthChanged UnityEvent; any UI component can subscribe and update its display without PlayerHealth knowing about UIManager. This reduces tight coupling: you can replace UIManager with a different implementation or add other listeners like audio cues and save systems with minimal change. A common mistake is to have PlayerHealth call UIManager. UpdateHealthBar directly; that creates a hard dependency and makes reuse difficult. Using interfaces is another option: a damageable interface lets damage sources call TakeDamage without knowing player internals. Decoupling also supports unit testing because you can supply mock listeners instead of real UI in test scenes. When building these systems you'll encounter recurring pitfalls. First, tight coupling happens when scripts call each other directly; avoid placing UI updates inside gameplay scripts. Use UnityEvent or interfaces instead. Second, continuous polling of other components in Update is inefficient and brittle—subscribe to events where possible. Third, mixing transform-based translation with Rigidbody physics can cause collisions to behave oddly; choose a single motion model per object. Fourth, forgetting to unsubscribe listeners before destroying objects may lead to null reference exceptions or lingering callbacks; remove listeners in OnDestroy or use inspector-only subscriptions. Fifth, incorrect grounding checks—such as relying on tag-less objects—will break jumping; ensure ground objects carry the correct tag or use layer masks. For debugging, add Debug. Log statements for state transitions and event invocations, use the inspector to watch values, and test on multiple resolutions to validate UI.
